title: Known by the one He blesses
word: Known by the one He blesses
hook: He is known by whom He chooses to be known (Sukhmani 16)

segments.voice: Yesterday, beyond the three qualities, and your line: beyond the moods. Did you name a mood and let it pass like weather? Today is day five hundred, and the salok's last phrase is a fitting one for a milestone. Day five hundred.
screen: `BEYOND THE THREE QUALITIES — BEYOND THE MOODS.`

segments.voice: Five hundred days. If you've come this far, you've opened this path five hundred times, more than a year's worth of days. You might be tempted to think you've earned something: a certain level, a certain closeness, a certain understanding. And in a way you have. You know words and stories you didn't know. But the sixteenth ashtpadi ends its salok with a line that gently turns the milestone around. Knowing God, it says, isn't the kind of thing you collect, like miles on a running app. Today: known by the one He blesses.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED DAYS.` → `HAVE YOU EARNED SOMETHING?` → `NOT MILES ON A RUNNING APP.`

segments.voice: Here's the end of the salok, in paraphrase: Nanak, He makes Himself understood to the one with whom He is pleased. Bujhaae: He causes to understand. Suprasann: well pleased, delighted. So understanding God isn't something you seize. It's something given, by the One, to whomever the One delights in. The Sikh word for that giving is nadar: grace, the glance of favor, literally a look. Japji Sahib puts it in a famous pair: by karma, by your actions, you receive this body like a garment; by nadar, by grace, you find the gate of liberation. Both halves matter. Actions are real and they shape your life. But the final door opens from the other side. Now, this can sound unfair, or as if effort doesn't count. Sikhs don't read it that way. Look at how the whole tradition behaves: rising early, reciting the banis, serving in the langar, remembering the Name all day. That's a lot of effort. The effort isn't a payment that buys the grace. It's more like opening the curtains. You can't make the sun rise. But you can open the curtains, every morning, so that when the light comes, it gets in. That's how many Sikhs describe their own daily discipline. And the salok's picture of grace is not a wage but a glance: nadar, a look of favor, given where the One is pleased. The posture it points to is waiting with the curtains open, not grabbing and not keeping score.
screen: `BUJHAAE: HE MAKES IT UNDERSTOOD.` · `NADAR: GRACE, A GLANCE.` · `KARMA THE GARMENT, NADAR THE GATE.` · `EFFORT OPENS THE CURTAINS.` · then, large: `KNOWN BY GRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait, receptive. Sit with your hands open, palms up, resting on your knees. Don't try to feel anything special. Don't reach. Just be like a room with the curtains open in the early morning: ready for whatever light comes, and fine if it's still gray. Each time you notice yourself straining, open your hands a little more. If you pray, let Waheguru be the only word, and let even that be quiet. The bell holds the time.
Known by the one He blesses. Nadar, grace: the One makes Himself understood to whomever He delights in. Effort opens the curtains; grace is the light.
screen: `KNOWN BY THE ONE HE BLESSES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: known by grace. Today, notice one good thing that came to you without your earning it, and let it be a gift, not a reward. Day five hundred.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of nadar, God's grace, as what finally opens the way, while keeping up daily effort in nitnem, seva and simran; the sixteenth salok of Sukhmani Sahib ends on this note.

match.prompt: known by grace — tap the pairs.

myth: in this salok, understanding God is something you can collect by effort alone
the One makes Himself understood to whomever He delights in.
nadar literally means a look or glance
grace pictured as the One's glance of favor.
Sikhs read grace as making effort pointless
effort is like opening the curtains; it doesn't buy the light, but it lets it in.

fork.setup: you've practiced every day for five hundred days. by the sixteenth salok, what have you earned?
options: open curtains: readiness for a light that's given, not bought.
fork.reveal: Japji says karma brings the garment, nadar the gate. effort keeps the curtains open; grace is the light.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nadar, grace, the glance of favor; a word from Persian nazar, sight.

trapdoor: what you thought: if I practice enough, I'll get to know God.
what it means: practice opens you; the knowing itself is given by grace.
what a scholar hears: nadar comes from Persian nazar, glance; Japji pauri 4 sets karmee aavai kaprraa against nadree mokh duaar, and Sukhmani 16 echoes it with bujhaae and suprasann.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 16, salok (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 283)
Japji Sahib, pauri 4 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2)

notes: Japji pauri 4: karmee aavai kaprraa nadree mokh duaar, paraphrased; confirm the reading of karam here (actions vs. grace; some commentators read karam as grace).
Day 500 milestone mentioned lightly in review and hook.

Audit (2026-10-01): the teach cast the listener's 500 days in the app as the effort that opens the way to grace and ended on a slogan ('Ready.'); it now describes how Sikhs speak of their own discipline. The hook no longer assumes 500 consecutive days.
